svg.title: Three levels of test for an MCP server, and what each one cannot see
svg.desc: Three stacked panels, one per level, drawn on the same two-slot picture so that the only thing changing down the column is what sits between the slots. Level 1 is unit tests: a test box points straight at a box holding your own function, with nothing in the gap, and the caption reads no client, no server, no protocol. It catches every branch of your own logic and all the ranking, parsing, clamping and edge cases, and it cannot see the published input and output schema or the result shape and the isError flag. Level 2 is in-memory protocol tests, driven by a client constructed around the server object: a blue client box and a terracotta server box exchange a request and a response across a dashed line, one process with the real protocol path and no pipe. It catches published schemas and annotations and the resultType, structured content and isError fields, and it cannot see a stray print call corrupting standard output or anything else about the process boundary. Level 3 is a live host: the same two boxes exchange the same two messages, but the gap now holds a hard pair of rules marking two processes, with standard output carrying every frame. It catches the stray print on the protocol channel and the launch command and the configuration file, and what it cannot see is little, but it is manual, stateful and not deterministic, so it is not a continuous integration gate. Measured run times sit in each panel header: twenty-three unit tests in 1.48 seconds, twenty-eight in-memory protocol tests in 1.47 seconds, and minutes by hand for the live host. A closing line says each level catches what the one above it structurally cannot, and that level 2 is the one most servers are missing.
svg.text: Three levels of test, and what each one cannot see
Twenty-eight protocol tests cost the same as twenty-three plain ones. Level 2 is the one that is missing.
Unit tests on your own functions
no client, no server, no protocol
every branch of your own logic
the published input and output schema
one process, real protocol path, no pipe
A live host, running the real process
two processes, stdout carries every frame
a stray print() on the protocol channel
the launch command and the config file
little, but it is manual and stateful
not deterministic, so not a CI gate
Each level catches what the one above it structurally cannot. Level 2 is the one most servers are missing.
